A Subtype α p can implicitly coerce to it's .val when used in sites that expect a α, except for when the site is using infix notation like + where a typeclass is invoked.

def n : { n : Nat // n % 3 = 0 } := ⟨9, by trivial⟩

def f (x : Nat) := x * 2
-- works ✅
#check f n -- f n.val : Nat
#check Nat.add 2 n -- Nat.add 3 n.val : Nat
-- fails ❌
#check 2 + n -- failed to synthesize instance of type class HAdd Nat { n // n % 3 = 0 } ?m.5
#check n + 2 -- failed to synthesize instance of type class HAdd { n // n % 3 = 0 } Nat ?m.5

Given that Nat.add 2 n works, I would expect the symbolic form 2 + n to work.

1) Why doesn't it?
2) Could it ever be made to work?
I think this is reasonable behaviour as long as you don't specify that your 2 is a Nat.
Wouldn't it be reasonable to infer, or assume, that 2 is a Nat since n is typed as a subtype of Nat?
The more reasonable thing to infer is that 2 is also a subtype of Nat.
Hmm, which subtype you think we should infer? If we infer it as the same subtype as n, you would only be able to add other numbers that are divisible by 3 to n.

In Lean, a number literal can be of any type. Once Lean has made a guess for which type it is, it synthesizes the value using the OfNat type class. In this case there is no such instance. But in principle, you could add an OfNat { n : Nat // n % 3 = 0 } 2 instance, and then Lean would use this (though I wouldn't recommend actually doing that).

The recommended solution to your problem is to add a type annotation, e.g. (2 + n : Nat)

@Sven River I've considered making arithmetic operators coerce values out of subtypes. That seems like the most likely thing someone would want it to do, since it's very unlikely anyone has any reasonable arithmetic instances on Subtype itself, and I think it's a better pattern to make a custom structure in that case.
Is there a good reason that this isn't using a custom structure instead of Subtype?
In any case, I think that example is why I dropped the idea before, thanks for the reminder.

Ah, I think I understand what you were saying @Jovan Gerbscheid. When you said:

The more reasonable thing to infer is that 2 is also a subtype of Nat.

you were describing what is already the behavior, in this example Lean is trying to infer that 2 is also a Subtype of Nat.

When Lean sees 2 + n, it does not know what type 2 on the lhs is, but it does know that the rhs n is of type { n : Nat // n % 3 = 0 }, and the default assumption is that both operands are of the same type, so it tries to infer that 2 is also of type { n : Nat // n % 3 = 0 } (which isn't even definitionally possible), and it doesn't know how to construct a { n : Nat // n % 3 = 0 } from a 2.

It's trying to interpret as { n : Nat // n % 3 = 0 } + { n : Nat // n % 3 = 0 }. Is all of that correct, do I understand the mechanics right?

Kyle Miller said:

I've considered making arithmetic operators coerce values out of subtypes.

Do you mean at the language level, a change to the compiler, or do you mean something I could do as a user at the library level like a Coe or HAdd instance that I import into files to enable?

Regarding those examples in MathLib that @Aaron Liu posted, It sounds like you two are saying that they are examples of Subtypes which have arithmetic operations defined on themselves, for whatever reason, rather than on their internal vals, and so if we were to change Lean to assume that + on a Subtype always defers to the + on the .val within, that would break these real-world usage in Mathlib. Do I have that correct also?

If so, could we solve this tension by specifying priority / default behaviors? If a Subtype explicitly defines arithmetic operators on itself, like the InstCoeSortType example, then that takes precedence, otherwise Lean would attempt to interpret the operation in terms of the .val inside. So 2 + n would just work out of the box, because there is no Add defined on { n : Nat // n % 3 = 0 }, we resort to assuming the Add defined on .val : Nat.

Could this work as a solution that does not break existing codebases?
